Q: .NET regex to detect missing full stops in thumbnails captions on frwiki A:

This is a first draft, preliminary Find / Replace solution.
It relies mostly on your original regex.
A balanced-group section was injected in the caption section as it seems this is
the only place needed, but I could be wrong.

The premise here was to use a lookahead to find a valid parameter first.
Then it moves past any parameters to get to the Caption ond of those captions,
match only the one(s) that do dot have a period anywhere at the end.

Another point of interest is that past the lookahead, when it optionally matches
parameters, that itself is entirely enclosed in an atomic. (?> (?:\| parameters)* )
this is necessary so that if a block only contains one parameter, it won't give
that back just to satisfy a Caption segment.
This is an important necessity.

And some refactor versions below.

Replace with $1$2. to repair.

Q: Powershell convert Array of Objects into PSCustomObject A:

It seems like what you want is to take an object array and make a hashtable out of it to lookup each cidr. The question could be rephrased.

$list = 'Name,CIDR
sdc-MO,10.92.18.136/20
sdc-RM,10.77.6.34/20' | convertfrom-csv

$list | % { $hash = @{} } { $hash[$_.Name] = $_.CIDR }

$hash['sdc-mo']
10.92.18.136/20

$hash['sdc-rm']
10.77.6.34/20

Q: Azure databricks spark - write to blob storage A:

UPDATED ANSWER:

I found a much simpler way of accomplishing this using dbutils.fs.put. You would need to loop through each row of your DataFrame, calling dbutils.fs.put() for each row.

Assuming your input file (assumed CSV) with two columns looks something like:

filepath, stringValue
wasbs://container@myaccount.blob.core.windows.net/demo1.txt,"demo string 1"
wasbs://container@myaccount.blob.core.windows.net/demo2.txt,"demo string 2"
wasbs://container@myaccount.blob.core.windows.net/demo3.txt,"demo string 3"
wasbs://container@myaccount.blob.core.windows.net/demo4.txt,"demo string 4"
wasbs://container@myaccount.blob.core.windows.net/demo5.txt,"demo string 5"

You can use the following to loop through each row in your input DataFrame:

df = spark.read.option("header", True).csv("wasbs://container@myaccount.blob.core.windows.net/demo-data.csv")

rowList = df.rdd.collect()
for row in rowList:
  dbutils.fs.put(str(row[0]), str(row[1]), True)

The put method writes a given String out to a file, encoded in UTF-8, so using this you can loop through each record in your DataFrame, passing the first column in as the file path, and the second as the string contents to write to the file.

This also has the benefit of writing the string to a single file, so you don't need to go through the process of renaming and moving files.

OLD ANSWER:

Due to the distributed nature of Spark, writing a DataFrame to files results in a directory being created which will contain multiple files. You can use coalesce to force the processing to a single worker and file, whose name will start with part-0000.

DISCLAIMER: This is recommended only for small files, as larger data files can lead to out of memory exceptions.

To accomplish what you are attempting, you would need to loop through each row of your DataFrame, creating a new DataFrame for each row which contains only the string value you want written to the file.

Assuming your input file (assumed CSV) with two columns looks something like:

filepath, stringValue
wasbs://container@myaccount.blob.core.windows.net/demo1,"demo string 1"
wasbs://container@myaccount.blob.core.windows.net/demo2,"demo string 2"
wasbs://container@myaccount.blob.core.windows.net/demo3,"demo string 3"
wasbs://container@myaccount.blob.core.windows.net/demo4,"demo string 4"
wasbs://container@myaccount.blob.core.windows.net/demo5,"demo string 5"

You can use the following to loop through each row in your input DataFrame:

from pyspark.sql import *
from pyspark.sql.types import StringType

df = spark.read.option("header", True).csv("wasbs://container@myaccount.blob.core.windows.net/demo-data.csv")

rowList = df.rdd.collect()
for row in rowList:
  dfRow = spark.createDataFrame([str(row[1])], StringType())
  dfRow.coalesce(1).write.mode("overwrite").text(row[0])

This will result in directories being created in your Blob Storage account container named demo1, demo2, demo3, demo4, and demo5. Each of those will contain multiple files. The file within each directory whose name begins with part-0000 is the file that will contain your string value.

If you need those files to have different names, and be in a different location, you can then use dbutils.fs methods to handle moving the files and doing the renames. You can also use this to do any cleanup of the directories that were created, if desired.

Q: Scaling a large Next.js SaaS frontend: architecture before introducing tests? A:

For the system you described, I would not pause for a big architecture cleanup before adding tests. I'd do both, but in a very uneven way: start tests immediately on the highest-risk tenant and business-rule flows, and refactor incrementally as you touch those areas. The reason is that a rewrite-first approach delays the safety net, while tests-without-boundaries will lock in some mess but still reduce risk now. The answer changes if tenant differences are mostly just config; if they're structurally different flows, I'd separate those earlier instead of trying to hide them behind one generic UI path.

On structure, the pattern I would pick is a layered frontend with real business boundaries: Next.js pages/components -> feature or application services -> domain model and tenant policy -> GraphQL adapter -> backend APIs. That works better than letting pages own orchestration, rules, and API shaping at once. The tradeoff is extra indirection, but that's exactly what makes domain rules testable and stops regressions from leaking across the app.

For separation, keep UI dumb enough to render state and raise intents, keep state management focused on screen/session state, keep GraphQL in adapter code that translates queries and mutations into app-facing models, and keep business logic in plain domain/application code. In practice that means pricing rules, entitlement checks, tenant-specific behavior, workflow decisions, and validation rules should not live in React components or GraphQL hooks. State should answer "what does this screen currently know," while domain code answers "what is allowed and what should happen."

Between the named approaches, I'd take vertical slices for feature ownership and discovery, but put Clean Architecture or DDD-inspired boundaries inside the slices where the logic is real. Feature-Sliced Design is fine as a repo organization scheme, but I would not rely on folder taxonomy alone to solve logic sprawl. A richer domain model is worth it for multi-tenant rule-heavy areas; for simple CRUD-ish flows, thin application services are enough. Pick this, document why, and revisit when a slice starts growing policy and workflow complexity.

With zero coverage, I would start with a small pyramid: a few end-to-end tests for the core money/permission/tenant journeys, then many fast tests at the domain and application-service layer, and only a modest number of component tests. Don't try to test everything through the browser first; that gets slow and brittle fast. I would explicitly add regression tests for cross-tenant behavior and role/authorization cases, because those are the easiest to break during refactors. Fowler's practical test pyramid is still a good mental model here, and OWASP's authorization regression testing cheat sheet is useful for thinking through the nasty permission edges.

Q: What is a user agent stylesheet? A:

Answering the question in title, what is the user agent stylesheet, the set of default styles in the browser. Here are some of them:

  • Chromium (Chrome): https://github.com/chromium/chromium/blob/main/third_party/blink/renderer/core/html/resources/html.css

  • WebKit (Safari): https://github.com/WebKit/WebKit/blob/main/Source/WebCore/css/html.css

  • Gecko (Firefox): https://github.com/mozilla-firefox/firefox/blob/main/layout/style/res/html.css

  • Ladybird: https://github.com/LadybirdBrowser/ladybird/blob/master/Userland/Libraries/LibWeb/CSS/Default.css

  • Servo: https://github.com/servo/servo/blob/main/components/layout/stylesheets/user-agent.css

Personal opinion: Don't fight with them. They have good default values, for example, in rtl/bidi cases and are consistent nowadays. Reset what you see irrelevant to you, not all of them at once.

Q: Why does C++ not "take care" of virtual base class moves, itself, with defaulted move assignments? A:

Note: this answer used to be incorrect (it might still be). The old version is preserved below for reference. Since the standard still allows (but does not require) that multiple assignment occurs, the old version might still be useful in determining what happens and why if multiple assignment occurs.

The standard says:

It is unspecified whether subobjects representing virtual base classes are assigned more than once by the implicitly-defined copy/move assignment operator

This wording was changed in C++14. Before that the situation was different.

It is unspecified whether subobjects representing virtual base classes are assigned more than once by the implicitly-defined copy assignment operator

and

A defaulted copy/move assignment operator for class X is defined as deleted if X has: [...] for the move assignment operator [...] any direct or indirect virtual base class.

Note the current wording only applies to implicitly defined move assignment operators, not explicitly defaulted ones.

See the resolution in WG21 N3833.

Usually when the standard explicitly says that something is unspecified, it means that specifying that thing would be too much strain for implementations. I don't know what was the exact rationale for leaving this unspecified, but the fact that there was a change implies that the thing was considered by the standards committee. If the standard explicitly leaves something unspecified, it usually means that specifying it would put too much strain on the implementation.

Old incorrect version

This is the chain of causes and effects.

  1. gcc warns you because you wrote code that is well-known not to work as you expect (i.e. move-from the virtual base exactly once).
  2. The code doesn't work as you expect because making it so would require changes in the language that no one is willing to make.
  3. No one is willing to make those changes because very few people need them, and the cost to benefit ratio is either unknown or bad.

What are those changes?

One possible way of changing the language is making the defaulted move assignment of D work as you expect if and only if move assignments of B and C are either implicitly defaulted or explicitly defaulted such that =default is visible to the move constructor of D. This can be argued to be (a) too complicated, because it is a special case in the language for a feature that is almost never used, and (b) fragile, because adding =default in a wrong place, or making the move assignment non-default, would silently break code.

Another possible change is to make the defaulted move assignment of D forbidden unless it can be made to work as you expect. This change is very simple and consistent, but it would prohibit useful and valid use cases. There is nothing wrong with moving-from an object more than once if that object doesn't in fact manage any resources.

If you want the move constructor of D work as you expect in more broad circumstances, this would require more profound changes, with very probable breakage of existing code. Or at least I cannot imagine how it possibly can be done. If you can, I encourage you to write a proposal.
